To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The hemodynamic response to a global hypercapnia manipulation is lower in older compared to younger adults.

1) the amplitude of the BOLD response to hypercapnic manipulation in the elderly is lower than in younger cohorts, 2) this is likely related to lower cerebral blood flow in the elderly and 3) this suggests that the same amplitude of BOLD response in an older subject could represent a larger neuronal activation than the same response in a younger subject.
the hemodynamic response to a cognitive task in older adults was similar to younger adults, but the response to a global hypercapnia challenge was significantly reduced.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of brain activity in the elderly.
the relationship between neuronal activation and the hemodynamic signal.
the study of the human cerebral cortex and its role in cognitive aging.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BOLD signal is not a direct and reliable index of neuronal activity.
the hemodynamic responses to cognitive tasks are similar in young and elderly adults but that the BOLD signal in the elderly may be less sensitive to neuronal activation.
BOLD signal changes in the brain are not a direct index of neural activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BOLD signal is a good measure of neuronal activity, but it is not a good measure of blood flow or oxygen consumption.
the hemodynamic response characteristics (HRC) are age dependent and the age related changes in HRC are not linear.
the BOLD response to a task is similar between young and old but the underlying hemodynamic response is different.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between BOLD and neuronal activation might be different in older and younger adults.
the relationship between BOLD and neuronal activity might not be the same in older and younger adults and that BOLD responses should be interpreted cautiously when comparing across populations.

the BOLD signal in older adults might reflect a greater degree of neuronal activity than the BOLD signal observed in younger adults and this should be taken into account when comparing BOLD responses between age groups.
